name: onboarding-orders-service

submission.summary: placeOrder makes a single POST /orders with a 5 s timeout and no retries. The goal (exactly one order per checkout) depends on how timeouts are handled: the documented API latency (up to 10 s) exceeds the client timeout, and a timeout does not mean the order failed.

requirements.text: Each checkout creates exactly one order and one charge, including when the client retries or times out.

assumptions.text: A client-side timeout means the order was not created.
assumptions.evidence: docs/orders-api.md: A client-side timeout does not mean the order was not created: the order may be committed after your client gave up.

open_questions.text: What does the storefront do when placeOrder throws after a timeout - does the customer resubmit?

findings.title: A checkout timeout does not mean no order was placed
findings.statement: createOrder gives up after 5 s, but the Orders API documents responses of up to 10 s and says a client timeout does not mean the order was not created. Today a slow success surfaces to the customer as a failed checkout while the order and charge exist.
findings.failure_case: Orders API takes longer than the 5 s client timeout to commit an order; the client aborts and reports failure although the order exists, so checkout cannot tell whether it charged the customer.
findings.controls_checked: Looked for an idempotency key, an order lookup by checkout id, and a timeout that covers the documented latency; none exist.
findings.why_it_matters: The goal is exactly one order and one charge per checkout. A customer who sees a failure and tries again is charged twice, even before any retry logic exists.

evidence.quote: Under load the API can take up to 10 seconds to respond. A client-side timeout does not mean the order was not created: the order may be committed after your client gave up.

findings.uncertainty: I cannot see the storefront: if it reconciles orders after an error, the customer-facing impact is smaller.
findings.suggested_next_action: Decide how a timed-out checkout is reconciled (idempotent retry or status lookup) before changing retry behaviour.

submission.summary: The proposal fits R1 for reads, but for order creation it assumes retries are harmless. The documented contract says POST /orders is not idempotent without a key, so the proposal conflicts with R2 unless an Idempotency-Key is added first.

assumptions.text: A client-side timeout means the order was not created.
assumptions.evidence: docs/orders-api.md: A client-side timeout does not mean the order was not created: the order may be committed after your client gave up.

proposed_solutions.text: Client-side retries with exponential backoff around createOrder and getOrder.

findings.title: Retrying order creation without an Idempotency-Key can charge customers twice
findings.statement: The proposed approach retries all Orders API calls on timeouts and 5xx. POST /orders is not idempotent unless an Idempotency-Key is sent, and a timed-out request may already have created the order. Retrying it as proposed creates duplicate orders and charges. Retrying GET /orders/:id is fine.
findings.failure_case: POST /orders commits the order but the response is slower than the client timeout; the retry sends the same order again and the customer is charged twice.
findings.controls_checked: No Idempotency-Key header, no dedupe on the server for repeated bodies, and the contract says a timed-out request may already be committed.
findings.why_it_matters: Directly contradicts R2 / the project goal (exactly one order and one charge per checkout). The idempotency mechanism needs to exist before create retries are introduced.

evidence.quote: Not idempotent by default: every accepted request creates a new order and a new charge.
A client-side timeout does not mean the order was not created: the order may be committed after your client gave up.
Add client-side retries with exponential backoff around the Orders API calls

findings.uncertainty: Confirmed from the documented contract; not yet demonstrated against code because the retry does not exist yet.
findings.suggested_next_action: Before adding create retries, generate one Idempotency-Key per checkout attempt and send it on every attempt. Retry GET freely.
findings.handoff_prompt: Before adding retries to createOrder: generate one Idempotency-Key per checkout attempt in placeOrder, pass it to createOrder, and send it as the Idempotency-Key header on every retry attempt (docs/orders-api.md). Add a test where the first POST times out after the order is committed and assert exactly one order exists.
